content: 1. The diagnostic approaches for tuberculosis (TB) in both adults and children include the use of commercial serodiagnostic tools, such as Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra, as initial tests for individuals presenting with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB. These tests are also recommended for adolescents and children with extrapulmonary TB symptoms. 2. Repeated testing with Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra is advised for children and adolescents showing signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB to improve diagnostic accuracy. 3. For adults in the general population, Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra are recommended as initial diagnostic tests for pulmonary TB, particularly in those with TB symptoms, chest radiography abnormalities, or both. 4. Truenat MTB, MTB Plus, and Truenat MTB-RIF Dx are additional diagnostic tools recommended for adults and children with pulmonary TB symptoms. 5. Moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are utilized for detecting TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification and lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assays are also diagnostic options. 6. Low-complexity NAATs are employed to detect resistance to isoniazid and second-line TB agents. First-line and second-line line-probe assays (LPAs and SL-LPAs) are used for identifying drug resistance, including pyrazinamide resistance, through high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs. 7. Treatment regimens for TB in children include specific approaches for severe pulmonary TB, TB in infants aged 0–3 months, and osteoarticular TB. Fixed-dose combination tablets and thrice-weekly dosing are recommended for ease of administration. 8. Corticosteroids are advised for managing TB meningitis. A four-month treatment regimen comprising isoniazid, rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide is recommended for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB. 9. For rifampicin-susceptible and isoniazid-resistant TB, specific regimens are outlined. Shorter all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline are recommended for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), while longer regimens are available for more complex cases. 10. The bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) regimen is recommended for MDR-TB cases with additional fluoroquinolone resistance. Monitoring patient response to MDR-TB treatment using culture methods is emphasized. 11. Models of TB care include health education, counseling, treatment adherence interventions, and ambulatory care for MDR-TB patients. Decentralized care models are also encouraged for better accessibility. 12. Routine HIV testing is recommended for individuals with presumptive or diagnosed TB. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is advised for infants, children, and adolescents living with HIV. 13. Guidelines emphasize the timing and eligibility for antiretroviral therapy (ART) in children and adolescents with TB, including first-line and second-line ART regimens. 14. Management of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and moderate undernutrition is critical in TB care. Contact investigation and preventive treatment for child contacts under five years of age are highlighted. 15. The 2022 WHO consolidated guidelines on TB management in children and adolescents incorporate evidence-based recommendations across the entire cascade of care, aiming to prevent TB, improve case detection, and optimize treatment outcomes. 16. The guidelines address the significant case detection gap in children due to challenges in specimen collection and bacteriological confirmation, particularly in young children with paucibacillary TB disease. 17. The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated the TB notification gap, with a 24% decrease in child TB notifications in 2020 compared to 2019. Efforts to close this gap include improving access to preventive treatment and high-quality care. 18. The guidelines focus on children and adolescents aged 0–19 years, emphasizing evidence-based interventions to reduce TB transmission, enable early diagnosis, and optimize treatment outcomes. 19. The 2022 update consolidates new and existing recommendations, including those from the 2014 guidelines, to provide a comprehensive framework for TB management in children and adolescents. 20. The target audience for these guidelines includes national TB programs, primary healthcare providers, pediatricians, clinicians, and organizations involved in TB, HIV, and infectious disease management. 21. The guidelines aim to align with global targets, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the WHO End TB Strategy, to reduce TB incidence and mortality by 2030.
